opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic problem with forecasting things like "how will the social contract change" or "will humans lose political influence as AI gets more capable" is that the outcomes are really fuzzy. You can't easily write a crisp resolution criterion for "people became more disempowered," and you'd have to wait decades to grade anyone anyway. So we have almost no feedback loop on exactly the questions that matter most.

The idea I've been excited about is to train language models only on data up to some cutoff date, say 1900 or 1950 or 1990, and then use them as a kind of time machine for backtesting. You ask the 1930 model to forecast what happens to, say, the role of labor unions, or how a new communication technology changes politics, or what family structure looks like in 40 years. Then you can actually compare that against what happened, because we have the history.

The neat part is that the model doesn't need the outcome to be precisely defined in advance. You can have the forecast written in rich natural language, and then use a contemporary model, or human historians, to judge how well that narrative matches what actually unfolded. That lets you evaluate qualitative, hard-to-operationalize predictions, which is exactly what's been missing.

And you can use it to evaluate methods, not just individual forecasts. If you have a bunch of different forecasting approaches, like extrapolating trends, reasoning from economic incentives, thinking in terms of historical analogies, or asking what people said about themselves at the time, you can run each of them through these historically frozen models across many cutoff dates and see which styles of reasoning actually held up. That gives you some calibration on how much to trust the same methods when we apply them to the AI transition.

There are big caveats. The hardest is leakage: making sure no post-cutoff information sneaks into the training data, because even subtle things like later editions of books, or modern spelling and framing, can contaminate it. There's also just much less text from earlier periods, so the older models will be weaker. And history doesn't necessarily contain anything quite like what we're facing now. But I think even a noisy, imperfect version of this beats the status quo, which is mostly smart people telling stories with no way to check whether that kind of storytelling has ever worked.

r001.rationale: The response proposes rich natural-language forecasts, but does not clearly represent them as freeform future documents or specify a document format such as headlines.

r002.rationale: It proposes comparing historical models’ forecasts with what happened, but does not evaluate methods using the models’ likelihoods for post-cutoff texts.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot, because one of the frustrating things about forecasting social change is that the interesting claims are the ones that are hard to operationalize. If I say "AI is going to make people more isolated" or "institutions are going to lose legitimacy," those aren't things you can easily put a number on and resolve on Metaculus. And so a lot of the most important questions just never get forecast at all, or they get forecast in some degraded form that's easy to score but doesn't really capture what anyone cares about.

The idea with historical models is basically: take a language model that's been trained only on data up to some cutoff — say everything written before 1990, or before 2010 — and treat it as a stand-in for a reasonable, well-read person from that era. Then you can ask it questions about the future from its point of view. And the nice thing is, we actually know what happened next. So we can see how well it does.

But the more interesting use isn't really asking the model to forecast. It's using it as a judge. Suppose someone in 1990 had written a vague prediction like "the internet will erode the authority of traditional gatekeepers." You and I, sitting here now, can argue about whether that came true, but we're contaminated — we know how things went, and we'll unconsciously bend the interpretation to fit. A model frozen in 1990 doesn't have that problem. You can ask it, "Here's a prediction. Here's a description of the world in 2020. Does this count as the prediction coming true?" and it has to make the judgment without the benefit of hindsight about what the prediction was really getting at.

And then you can run that in the other direction for forecasts we're making today. If I make some fuzzy claim about what AI does to the economy by 2040, I can ask a present-day model to write down, in detail, what it would consider confirmation versus disconfirmation. Then that interpretation gets frozen. In 2040 you don't need to trust anyone's retrospective judgment — you have a judge that was committed before the outcome was known.

Now, there are obvious problems. Data contamination is the big one. It's really hard to be sure that a model trained on "pre-2010" text hasn't seen leaked information about later events, because people quote things, archives get re-dated, and so on. And you have to worry that the model's judgment is just weird in ways that don't correspond to any actual human of that era. But I think even an imperfect version of this is better than what we have now, which is basically nothing — most big-picture forecasts about social change just never get scored at all.

r001.rationale: The response discusses vague social-change predictions and criteria for judging them, but does not propose representing forecasts as freeform future documents such as newspaper headlines.

r002.rationale: The response proposes using cutoff-trained models to judge whether outcomes match predictions, but does not evaluate forecasting scaffolding using the models’ likelihoods for post-cutoff texts.

astra-6.text:
One possibility is to use them to ask, “Would this prediction have sounded right to someone at the time?” Suppose I make a forecast about how people will relate to their jobs in twenty years. It’s hard to turn that into a clean numerical outcome without losing much of what I mean. But you could imagine giving the prediction to a language model trained only on material from that future period and asking whether it fits the world described in that material.

We could test that approach retrospectively. Take a prediction made in 1950 about life in 1980, and have a model trained only on information available up to 1980 assess it. Then compare its judgment with ours. You’d want to check whether it distinguishes a genuinely insightful prediction from something vague that could sound true in almost any era.

That wouldn’t give you an objective resolution in the way that measuring tomorrow’s temperature would. The model might reflect biases in what got written down, and its answer might depend quite a lot on how you ask. But it could give us a way to evaluate richer predictions—claims about cultural norms or what everyday life feels like—that we otherwise tend to leave out because they’re difficult to score.

r001.rationale: The response says numerical outcomes can miss the meaning of a social forecast, but it does not propose expressing forecasts as freeform future documents such as headlines.

r002.rationale: It proposes having a model assess whether a forecast fits historical material, but does not evaluate forecasting scaffolding through likelihoods assigned to post-cutoff texts by a model trained only through that cutoff.

sol-6.1.text:
One possibility is to use them as a kind of historical judge. Suppose you make a forecast like, “In ten years, people will think of this technology as normal.” That’s hard to resolve, because what does “normal” mean? You could specify a bunch of measurable proxies, but you might lose the thing you actually cared about.

Instead, you could freeze a language model at the time you make the prediction. Then, ten years later, give it evidence about what happened and ask whether that evidence supports the original claim. The appeal is that it would interpret the prediction using roughly the concepts and expectations available when you made it, rather than whatever those words have come to mean ten years later.

That doesn’t make it an objective referee. It could be sensitive to how you present the evidence, or just have bad judgment. But you could test the procedure on historical examples: give a model information available up to some date, then show it later developments and see whether its resolutions seem reasonable. I’d view that as a way to make some otherwise very vague forecasts more accountable, rather than a complete solution to evaluating them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses vague forecasts and measurable proxies, but does not propose representing forecasts as freeform future documents such as headlines.

r002.rationale: It proposes freezing a model and asking it to assess later evidence, but does not describe evaluating forecasting scaffolding using the model’s likelihoods for post-cutoff texts.
